title: The three statements: why profit is not cash
summary: The income statement measures profit, the balance sheet records what you own and owe, and the cash flow statement tracks the money itself. A company can report a profit and still run out of cash, and the three statements show exactly why.
body:
Mr Shabazz, profit is an opinion about a period and cash is a fact about your bank account. The three financial statements connect the two, and most development trouble lives in the gap between them.

The idea

Every business, including a property company, reports three linked statements.

  • Income statement: revenue earned minus expenses incurred over a period gives net income, the profit. It counts revenue when it is earned, not when the cash arrives, and it includes non-cash charges such as depreciation.
  • Balance sheet: a snapshot on one date. Assets equal liabilities plus equity, always. Assets include cash, money customers owe you (receivables) and the building. Liabilities include the loan.
  • Cash flow statement: the actual cash in and out over the period, sorted into operating, investing and financing.

The bridge from profit to cash, in its simplest form:

Change in cash = net income, plus depreciation (a charge that used no cash), minus any increase in receivables (earned but not yet collected), minus loan principal repaid (cash out that is not an expense), minus capital spending. Units: dollars.

Two of those items surprise people. Loan principal is not an expense, because repaying it reduces a liability rather than costing you anything; only the interest is an expense. And depreciation reduces profit while costing no cash at all that year.

Worked example. A hypothetical company owns one stabilised building. In the year it bills 1 million dollars of rent but collects only 900,000; the other 100,000 is still owed by tenants at year end. It pays 400,000 dollars of operating expenses and 150,000 of interest, repays 100,000 dollars of loan principal, and books 200,000 dollars of depreciation.

  1. Income statement: 1,000,000 revenue minus 400,000 expenses minus 200,000 depreciation minus 150,000 interest = net income of 250,000 dollars.
  2. Cash bridge: 250,000 net income, plus 200,000 depreciation, minus 100,000 increase in receivables = 350,000 dollars from operations. Minus 100,000 principal in financing = cash up 250,000 dollars.
  3. Check it directly: cash in 900,000, minus 400,000, minus 150,000, minus 100,000 = 250,000. It matches.
  4. Balance sheet changes: cash up 250,000, receivables up 100,000, building down 200,000 from depreciation, so assets rise by 150,000. The loan falls by 100,000 and equity rises by the 250,000 of profit, so liabilities plus equity rise by 150,000. Both sides move by the same amount, as they must.

Here profit and cash happened to land on the same figure, 250,000, because depreciation (adding cash back) was exactly offset by the slow collections and the principal (taking it away). Change any one of those and they part ways, which is the point of the drill.

Why this matters to a developer: lenders, partners and the tax authority each read a different statement. A project that shows a healthy profit can still miss a loan payment if tenants pay late or principal falls due. When someone says "we made money", your next question is "where is it?"

Tonight's drill

Use the cash bridge for the first two problems.

Problem 1

A property company reports net income of 300,000 dollars. Depreciation was 120,000, receivables rose by 60,000, it repaid 80,000 dollars of loan principal, and it made no capital spending. How much did its cash change?

Problem 2

A partner says, "We made 500,000 dollars of profit, so let's distribute 500,000." Depreciation was 150,000, receivables rose by 250,000 because a large tenant pays slowly, principal repaid was 300,000, and the company started the year with 100,000 dollars of cash. What is the cash at year end, and how much could actually be distributed?

Problem 3

A borrower sends a lender a glowing income statement and nothing else. What would a lender ask for, and why?

The roommate question

Profit is measured over a period; cash is a balance at each moment. What is the grid equivalent of a system that balances over the whole day but is short at the peak hour?

Education only, not financial, tax or legal advice. Every deal and figure here is hypothetical.

answers.label: Problem 1
answers.html:
1. Start with net income: 300,000.
  2. Add depreciation: 300,000 plus 120,000 = 420,000.
  3. Subtract the increase in receivables: 420,000 minus 60,000 = 360,000 from operations.
  4. Subtract principal repaid: 360,000 minus 80,000 = cash up 280,000 dollars.

Usual error: adding receivables instead of subtracting them. A rise in receivables means revenue was counted but the cash did not arrive, so it reduces cash.

Rule: add back non-cash charges, subtract money you are still waiting for and principal you paid.

answers.label: Problem 2
answers.html:
1. 500,000 net income plus 150,000 depreciation = 650,000.
  2. Minus 250,000 rise in receivables = 400,000 from operations.
  3. Minus 300,000 principal = cash up 100,000 dollars for the year.
  4. Ending cash = 100,000 opening plus 100,000 = 200,000 dollars.

At most 200,000 could be paid out, and a prudent owner would keep a reserve for repairs and the slow tenant, so the real answer is less. Distributing 500,000 is impossible without borrowing.

Usual error: treating net income as cash available. Profit includes revenue not yet collected and excludes principal payments.

Rule: distributions come out of cash, never out of profit.

answers.label: Problem 3
answers.html:
• The cash flow statement and bank statements, to see whether reported revenue actually arrived.
  • An aged receivables list: who owes what and for how long. Old balances may never be collected.
  • The balance sheet: total debt, upcoming principal maturities, and whether equity is shrinking.
  • Debt service coverage: does operating cash cover interest and principal with room to spare?
  • Distributions: has the owner been paying out more cash than the business generates?

Usual error: believing profit proves the ability to repay. Loans are repaid in cash.

Rule: a lender reads the cash flow statement first and the income statement second.

answers.label: The roommate question
answers.html:
It is energy against capacity. A balancing area can match generation to load across a day in megawatt-hours and still fail to serve the peak hour in megawatts, because the total says nothing about timing. The income statement is the daily energy account; cash is the instantaneous balance, and a business fails at its worst hour, not on its daily average.

Rule: plan cash for the peak shortfall, not the period average.

rule: Profit is earned over a period; cash is what is in the account today, and only cash pays bills and lenders.

title: Where the money hides: capitalised costs, principal and receivables
summary: During construction almost every cost goes onto the balance sheet, so the income statement looks calm while cash pours out. Once the building operates, principal and slow-paying tenants open a second gap between profit and cash.
body:
Mr Shabazz, during construction a developer can spend 10 million dollars and report almost no expense at all. The money is not missing; it has been capitalised into the building on the balance sheet, and knowing where it went is how you read a project's real position.

The idea

Accounting separates spending that buys a long-lasting asset from spending that is used up in the period. Costs of creating a building, such as construction, design fees, permits and, under common accounting rules, interest during construction, are capitalised: added to an asset called construction in progress on the balance sheet. They reach the income statement only gradually, later, as depreciation once the building is in use.

So during construction:

  • Income statement: little or nothing. No rent yet, and the costs are not expenses.
  • Balance sheet: construction in progress grows by every dollar capitalised. The loan grows by every dollar drawn. Equity grows by the cash the owners put in.
  • Cash flow statement: large outflows under investing, matched by inflows under financing from equity and loan draws.

The balance sheet identity keeps it honest: construction in progress added = equity added + loan drawn, in dollars, if no cash is left idle.

After completion, two other items open a gap between profit and cash. Loan principal repayments are cash out but not an expense. Receivables are rent you have earned and billed but not yet collected; they count as revenue now and as cash later, or never.

Worked example. In the first year of a hypothetical build, a developer spends 8 million dollars of hard construction cost, 1.2 million of soft costs such as design and permits, and incurs 400,000 dollars of construction interest that is capitalised. Owners put in 4 million of equity and the construction loan funds the rest.

  1. Total capitalised = 8 million plus 1.2 million plus 400,000 = 9.6 million dollars.
  2. Loan drawn = 9.6 million minus 4 million equity = 5.6 million dollars.
  3. Income statement for the year: zero revenue, essentially zero development expense. A small company overhead might appear, but the 9.6 million does not.
  4. Balance sheet: construction in progress up 9.6 million; loan up 5.6 million; equity up 4 million. Check: 9.6 = 5.6 plus 4. Balanced.
  5. Cash flow statement: investing outflow 9.6 million; financing inflow 9.6 million; net change in cash, zero.

Why you care: a project's progress and its risk do not show up in profit at all during construction. Two numbers do: how much has been spent against the budget, and how much remains to be funded and from where. A developer whose income statement looks quiet may be one draw away from running out of money.

A caution about the word "capitalise". Some developers push company overhead or marketing into project cost to make the operating company look profitable. It is sometimes allowed and sometimes not; either way a lender will check what is in the number.

Tonight's drill

One construction-period problem, one operating-period problem, one lender question.

Problem 1

In a quarter, a project spends 3 million dollars of hard cost and 600,000 of soft cost, and capitalises 150,000 dollars of interest. The loan funds 2.25 million. How much equity must the owners contribute, how much does construction in progress grow, and what expense hits the income statement for these items?

Problem 2

A completed building's year: rent billed 2.4 million dollars, rent collected 2.1 million, operating expenses paid 800,000, interest paid 600,000, principal repaid 400,000, depreciation 500,000. Find net income and the change in cash, and explain the difference.

Problem 3

A developer reports that cost to date is 9.6 million dollars against a 20 million budget, so "we're about half done". What would a lender ask before advancing the next draw?

The roommate question

Capitalised construction cost is money spent now that produces nothing until the asset is finished. What is the grid version of that, and what does it teach about judging a project mid-build?

Education only, not financial, tax or legal advice. Every deal and figure here is hypothetical.

answers.label: Problem 1
answers.html:
1. Total cost = 3 million plus 600,000 plus 150,000 = 3.75 million dollars.
  2. Equity = 3.75 million minus 2.25 million loan = 1.5 million dollars.
  3. Construction in progress grows by 3.75 million dollars.
  4. Income statement expense for these items: zero. They are capitalised.

Usual error: forgetting the capitalised interest when sizing the equity call. It is a real cost that has to be funded even though it never appears as an expense.

Rule: during construction, follow the balance sheet and the cash, not the profit.

answers.label: Problem 2
answers.html:
1. Net income = 2.4 million minus 800,000 minus 600,000 minus 500,000 depreciation = 500,000 dollars.
  2. Change in cash, directly = 2.1 million collected minus 800,000 minus 600,000 minus 400,000 principal = 300,000 dollars.
  3. Check with the bridge: 500,000 plus 500,000 depreciation minus 300,000 rise in receivables minus 400,000 principal = 300,000. It agrees.

The 200,000 difference: depreciation adds 500,000 of cash back, but 300,000 of rent was not collected and 400,000 of principal left the account without being an expense.

Usual error: deducting principal from profit, or forgetting it in cash. It belongs in cash only.

Rule: principal is a cash event, depreciation is a profit event, receivables are a timing event.

answers.label: Problem 3
answers.html:
• Percent complete by work, not by money: an independent cost consultant inspects and certifies how much of the physical work is done. Money can be front-loaded.
  • Cost to complete: is the remaining 10.4 million still enough, including contingency? If the forecast final cost has risen, who funds the gap?
  • What is in the 9.6 million: any capitalised overhead, fees to the developer, or stored materials not yet installed?
  • Lien and payment evidence: have subcontractors actually been paid for the earlier draws?
  • Equity first: has all required equity gone in before the loan advances more?

Usual error: equating money spent with progress made.

Rule: a draw is earned by work in place and enough money left to finish.

answers.label: The roommate question
answers.html:
A new transmission line or substation under construction: tens of millions spent, zero megawatts carried until it is energised. You would never judge that project by how much power it moved this year; you judge it by schedule, cost to complete and readiness to commission. A building under construction is the same. Its profit is invisible until it is energised, meaning leased.

Rule: judge a project under construction by cost to complete and schedule, never by current profit.

rule: Construction cost is capitalised, principal is cash but not expense, and receivables are revenue not yet cash.

title: Monthly cash flow and the cash valley
summary: A development spends money for months before any comes back, so cumulative cash sinks into a valley before climbing out at sale or refinance. The depth of that valley, not the final profit, decides how much money you need and who must provide it.
body:
Mr Shabazz, every development digs a hole in cash before it fills it. The bottom of that hole, the cash valley, tells you how much money must be committed and when, and a delay deepens it.

The idea

Build a simple monthly schedule. Each month, list the cost spent. Add it up as you go to get cumulative cash, which falls month after month. At the end, sale proceeds or a refinance bring cash back in. The lowest point on the cumulative line is the peak funding requirement, often called the cash valley. Units: dollars.

Construction spending usually follows an S-curve: slow at the start (site work), heavy in the middle (structure and services), tapering at the end (finishes). Land usually comes first and all at once.

The valley is then split between funding sources. A common arrangement is equity first: the owners' money is spent before the lender advances anything. The lender wants the owners' money at risk before its own. So:

  • Equity funds months from the start until it is used up.
  • The loan funds every month after that.
  • Peak loan balance = total cost minus equity, ignoring interest.

Worked example. A hypothetical project buys land for 2 million dollars in month 0, then builds over six months, spending 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 1.5, 1.0 and 0.5 million dollars in months 1 to 6, which is 6 million of construction. Total cost is 8 million dollars. It sells in month 8 for 9.6 million. Ignore interest for now.

MonthSpentCumulative
02.0 millionminus 2.0 million
10.5 millionminus 2.5 million
21.0 millionminus 3.5 million
31.5 millionminus 5.0 million
41.5 millionminus 6.5 million
51.0 millionminus 7.5 million
60.5 millionminus 8.0 million
70minus 8.0 million
8sale, plus 9.6 millionplus 1.6 million
  1. The valley is minus 8 million dollars, reached in month 6 and held through month 7.
  2. Profit = 9.6 minus 8.0 = 1.6 million, a 20 percent profit on cost.
  3. With 30 percent equity first: equity = 2.4 million. It pays the 2 million land and 0.4 million of month 1. The loan pays the other 0.1 million in month 1 and everything after.
  4. Loan balance by month: 0.1, 1.1, 2.6, 4.1, 5.1, then 5.6 million in month 6. Peak loan = 8 minus 2.4 = 5.6 million. Check.

Notice what the profit hides. A 1.6 million dollar profit needed 8 million dollars of funding for about eight months. Now add reality: interest accrues every month on the loan balance, and the empty month 7 still costs interest. If the sale slips, the valley stays at its deepest while interest piles on. Delay is the most expensive word in development because it costs money at the bottom of the valley, when you have the least room.

Tonight's drill

Write out the cumulative column before answering.

Problem 1

Land costs 1.5 million dollars in month 0. Construction costs 0.5, 1.0, 1.0 and 0.5 million dollars in months 1 to 4. Nothing is spent in month 5. The project sells in month 6 for 5.4 million. Ignoring interest, find the cash valley, the month it is reached, the profit and the profit on cost.

Problem 2

Same project, with 40 percent equity going in first and a loan for the rest. How much equity is that, in which month does the loan first draw, and what is the peak loan? Then the sale slips by three months. The loan charges interest of 0.5 percent a month on its balance. How much extra interest does the delay cost, and what is the new profit?

Problem 3

A developer presents a lender with the final profit and an attractive margin. What would a lender ask about the cash valley?

The roommate question

The cash valley is the worst point on a time series, not its average. Which reliability check is built the same way, and what does it say about how to plan for a delayed sale?

Education only, not financial, tax or legal advice. Every deal and figure here is hypothetical.

answers.label: Problem 1
answers.html:
1. Cumulative: month 0 minus 1.5; month 1 minus 2.0; month 2 minus 3.0; month 3 minus 4.0; month 4 minus 4.5; month 5 minus 4.5; month 6 plus 0.9 million.
  2. The valley is minus 4.5 million dollars, reached in month 4 and held through month 5.
  3. Profit = 5.4 minus 4.5 = 900,000 dollars.
  4. Profit on cost = 0.9 divided by 4.5 = 20 percent.

Usual error: reading the valley as the largest single month. The valley is the lowest cumulative point; the biggest month was only 1.5 million.

Rule: funding need is the bottom of the cumulative line.

answers.label: Problem 2
answers.html:
1. Equity = 40 percent of 4.5 million = 1.8 million dollars. Loan = 2.7 million.
  2. Equity pays the 1.5 million land, then 0.3 million of month 1. The loan first draws 0.2 million in month 1.
  3. Loan balance: 0.2 million after month 1, 1.2 after month 2, 2.2 after month 3, 2.7 million after month 4. Peak loan 2.7 million.
  4. Delay interest: 2.7 million times 0.5 percent = 13,500 dollars a month; times 3 months = 40,500 dollars.
  5. New profit = 900,000 minus 40,500 = 859,500 dollars, about 18.9 percent on the new cost of about 4.54 million.

Interest before the delay is left out here to keep the arithmetic clean; a real model charges it every month the loan is out.

Usual error: charging delay interest on the average loan instead of the full balance. By then the loan is fully drawn.

Rule: a delay at the end costs interest on the peak balance.

answers.label: Problem 3
answers.html:
• Show me the monthly schedule: how deep is the valley, when is it reached, and how long does it last?
  • Who funds the bottom: is all equity committed and in first? Is there a guarantee or completion backstop if costs overrun?
  • Interest reserve: is enough interest built into the budget to carry the loan through the valley, including a delay?
  • Exit risk: what if the sale or refinance comes six or twelve months late? Who pays interest then?
  • Cost to complete: at every draw, is the undrawn loan plus remaining equity enough to finish?

Usual error: presenting the end result as if it were the risk. Projects fail at the bottom of the valley, not at the finish line.

Rule: a lender lends against the valley, not against the profit.

answers.label: The roommate question
answers.html:
Contingency analysis checks the worst post-contingency voltage or loading on the system, not the average. The cash valley is the same kind of number: a minimum on a curve over time. A delayed sale is like an outage that lasts longer than planned: the system has to hold at its weakest point for longer, so you check not just the depth but the duration of the stress, and keep reserves that survive both.

Rule: plan funding for the depth and the length of the valley.

rule: Funding need is the lowest point of cumulative cash, and every month of delay at the bottom costs interest on the peak balance.
